readerTitle: Three dry cleaners on one street: a year of pricing calls
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (한 거리의 세탁소 세 곳, 치과 체인 유니폼 계약) · 모든 수치와 상황은 설명용
insight: 한 가게도 상품마다 다른 시장 구조 안에 있다. 가격을 정하기 전에 '이 상품의 시장은 어떤 모양인가'를 먼저 본다.
misconception: 경쟁자가 있으면 가격을 더 낮추는 쪽이 이긴다. 그리고 한 사업은 하나의 시장에만 속한다.

sources.text: 미시경제학 표준 개념 (완전경쟁, 가격 수용자와 가격 설정자, 과점, 보완재)
모든 상황과 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 가격($3, $2.50, $2.25)과 거리(200미터)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 시장 데이터가 아닙니다.
6번 카드의 '경쟁사와 가격을 합의하는 것은 많은 나라의 경쟁법이 금지한다'는 일반적 설명입니다. 특정 국가의 법률 조언이 아니며, 문구가 일반론을 넘지 않는지 게시 전에 확인하세요.

cards.title: Three dry cleaners, one street, one price
body: On Elm Street, three dry cleaners sit within 200 meters of each other. All three charge $3 to clean a shirt.
You just bought the middle one. Over the next year you'll make four calls. Each one tests a different idea about how markets work.

image.label: Three small dry cleaners side by side on one street
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 한 거리에 나란히 선 작은 세탁소 세 곳. 세 곳 모두 창문에 "Shirts $3" 표지. 가운데 가게만 살짝 밝은 조명으로 강조. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How do you price a shirt?
body: Customers see the three shops as the same. A clean shirt is a clean shirt, and the next shop is a one-minute walk away.
You want to grow fast. What do you charge?

options.text: $2.50, to pull customers from both rivals
options.feedback: Your banner is visible from both shops. Within a week they match, and all three earn less on every shirt.
You keep steady volume and a normal margin. For an identical service, the street sets the price and you accept it.

options.text: $3.75, because your shop is newly renovated
options.feedback: Nice paint doesn't change the shirt. Customers walk 100 meters and you lose regulars.

cards.title: Where can you set your own price?
body: Say you chose $3. Business is steady, but shirts leave a thin margin and you can't raise their price alone.
You have a skilled tailor on staff two days a week. What do you add?

options.text: Same-day alterations and repairs, which neither rival offers
options.feedback: Nobody nearby can do it, so you set this price yourself. Repair jobs soon earn more per hour than shirts.
It wins some late commuters, but a rival can copy it next Monday. It adds cost without giving you pricing room.

options.text: A loyalty card: tenth shirt free
options.feedback: It's a 10% price cut in disguise. Rivals launch their own cards and the street's margin shrinks again.

cards.title: A rival cuts shirts to $2.50.
body: Say you added alterations. Six months later, the shop on the corner hangs a banner: *Shirts $2.50*.
Many of your repair jobs come from people dropping off shirts. How do you respond?

options.text: Hold at $3 and rely on your alterations
options.feedback: You keep the shirt margin, but fewer people walk in. Repair orders slip, because shirts were bringing those customers to you.

options.text: Match $2.50 on shirts only, keep alteration prices
options.feedback: You protect the foot traffic that feeds your profitable service without starting a deeper fight. The corner shop gains little and the war stalls.

options.text: Go to $2.25 and win the street
options.feedback: With only three shops, every move gets answered. The third shop follows, and soon nobody earns money on shirts.

cards.softwareNote: Software has the same pattern. Basic features in a crowded category behave like shirts: a few rivals watch each other's pricing pages and match fast. Pricing room usually lives in the parts only you offer, such as a special integration or workflow.

cards.title: A clinic chain wants a uniform contract.
body: Say you matched on shirts. A chain of four dental clinics asks all three shops to bid on cleaning its staff uniforms every week.

options.text: The lowest price per item you can stand
options.feedback: You may win, but on price alone. Next year a rival bids a cent lower and the contract leaves with them.

options.text: The normal price, plus weekly pickup, delivery and free repairs
options.feedback: The package is hard to compare line by line, and only you can include repairs. The clinics choose on convenience, and switching later means losing the repairs.

options.text: Decline. Business contracts aren't your trade
options.feedback: You stay focused, but your machines sit idle midweek. That capacity could have earned money with little added cost.

cards.title: One shop, three different markets.
body: Notice that your shop never sat in just one market. Plain shirts behaved like a **commodity**: identical service, many nearby options, a price you had to accept.
Alterations were nearly yours alone, so you could set the price. And the shirt price war was a small-group contest, where each move gets answered.
The right pricing move depended less on your costs than on **which market each service was in**.

image.label: One shop split into three zones: shirts, alterations, contracts
image.brief: 가운데 세탁소 단면을 세 구역으로 나눈 인포그래픽. "Shirts: price set by the street", "Alterations: price set by you", "Contracts: price set by bidding". 각 구역마다 다른 색. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Advantages fade, and matching has a line.
body: Your alteration edge lasts only until a rival hires a tailor. Special services need refreshing, or they slowly become commodities too.

And there's a line between watching rivals and talking to them. Seeing a banner and responding is normal competition. Agreeing with rivals on prices is collusion, which competition laws in many countries forbid.

cards.title: Before you set a price, ask what kind of market that product is in.
body: Here is how your four calls map to this unit:
list: **Shirts at $3:** a commodity, so you were a price taker
**Alterations:** something only you offered, so you were a price maker
**Matching the cut:** few rivals watching each other, an oligopoly
**The uniform bid:** shirts and repairs as complements that make your offer hard to replace
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list your top three products. For each, write whether customers could get the same thing next door.
